title: OPERATING SYSTEMS
body:
The operating system is the layer between programs and hardware. It decides which process
runs next, stops concurrent processes from corrupting each other's data, hands out memory
and pretends there's more of it than exists, and turns a disk into files and directories.

The spine of this course is **[[Synchronization]]**. Most of the material builds toward
the [[Critical Section Problem]] and the mechanisms that solve it. It sits directly on top
of [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (interrupts, I/O, context switching) and reuses data
structures from [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]].

## Topics

### System structure

[[Operating System Structure]]: how the kernel is organised and what runs privileged.
Builds on [[Kernel]], [[System Call]], and [[Supervisor State]] from second year.

### Processes

[[Processes]] · [[PCB]] · [[Process State]] · [[Process Priority]] · [[Control Block]]

A process is tracked by its [[PCB]] and moves between states as it is scheduled, blocks on
I/O, or is woken. It always lives in a [[Queue]]: the [[Ready Queue]] when runnable, a
[[Wait Queue]] when blocked, entering a [[Waiting state]] until signalled.

### Threads and CPU scheduling

[[Thread]] · [[CPU Scheduling]] · [[Fairness]] · [[Starvation]] · [[Processor Affinity]] ·
[[Amdahl's Law]]

Scheduling policy trades throughput against [[Fairness]]; a policy that is unfair enough
lets a thread starve. [[Processor Affinity]] matters because a migrated thread arrives on a
CPU whose [[Cache]] knows nothing about it. [[Amdahl's Law]] is the ceiling on what adding
cores can buy you, and the serial fraction it refers to is precisely the [[Critical Section]].

### Synchronization, the core of the course

[[Synchronization]] · [[Concurrency]] · [[Critical Section]] · [[Critical Section Problem]]

The three requirements: [[Mutual Exclusion]], [[Progress]], [[Bounded Waiting]].

Solutions, weakest to strongest:

| Approach | Mechanism | Problem with it |
|---|---|---|
| [[Peterson's Solution]] | Software only, `flag[]` plus `turn` | Busy-waits; instruction order is fragile; doesn't scale past two processes |
| [[TAS]] | Atomic test-and-set instruction | Needs [[Hardware]] support; still a [[Spin Lock]] |
| [[Locks]] / [[Mutex Lock]] | Acquire, critical section, release | Blocking, but coarse |
| [[Semaphores]] | Counter plus [[Wait Queue]] | Correct and general; easy to misuse |

Classic problems: [[Bounded Buffer Problem]] ([[Producer Consumer]]).

### Inter-process communication

[[Inter-process Communication]] · [[Shared Memory]] · [[Message Passing]] ·
[[Process Communication]] · [[Piping]]

The two forms are shared memory (fast, but you own the synchronization) and message
passing (slower, but the kernel handles the coordination). [[Piping]] is the shell-level
form of message passing; see [[Shell]].

### Memory

[[Main memory]] · [[Virtual Memory]] · [[Memory Mapping]] · [[Address Space]]

Virtual memory is the illusion that each process has a large private address space.
Compare the concrete layout from first year: [[Stack and Heap]], [[Dynamic Allocation]],
[[Static Allocation]].

### Storage and file systems

[[File Systems]] · [[File System Interface]] · [[Mass Storage Structure]] · [[File]] ·
[[Directory]] · [[Buffering]] · [[Double Buffering]]

The interface (open, read, write, seek) versus the on-disk structures that implement it.
[[Buffering]] and [[Double Buffering]] carry over from [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]].

## Core Facts to Know

- A [[Processes|process]] is a program in execution, with its own address space.
- A [[Thread]] shares an address space with other threads in the same process.
- The [[PCB]] (Process Control Block) holds per-process state.
- The PCB is usually implemented as a doubly [[Linked List]].
- Every process sits in some [[Queue]], either a [[Ready Queue]] or a [[Wait Queue]].
- A [[Wait Queue]] is [[FIFO]].
- A [[Critical Section]] is code performing a transaction on a shared resource.
- A critical section must be serialized.
- The four parts of the loop are entry section, critical section, exit section, remainder section.
- [[Mutual Exclusion]] means at most one process is in a critical section at a time.
- [[Progress]] means only processes in the entry section take part in the admission decision.
- [[Bounded Waiting]] means time in the entry section has an upper bound.
- Bounded waiting is what prevents [[Starvation]].
- A correct solution to the critical section problem needs all three: mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting.
- [[Peterson's Solution]] is a software-only solution that works but is not good in practice.
- Peterson's solution busy-waits.
- Swapping the order of the flag assignment and the turn assignment in Peterson's solution breaks it.
- Hardware support is a better solution than a software-only one.
- [[TAS]] (test-and-set) is an atomic hardware instruction.
- A [[Spin Lock]] busy-waits while holding the CPU.
- A spin lock is only worth it when the expected wait is shorter than a context switch.
- A [[Semaphores|semaphore]] is a non-negative integer counter.
- A semaphore is associated with a [[Wait Queue]].
- Acquiring a lock when the semaphore is 0 puts the thread in a [[Waiting state]].
- Releasing a lock increments the counter *and* signals a waiting thread.
- A [[Mutex Lock]] is a binary semaphore; its counter is only ever 0 or 1.
- [[POSIX]] provides `sem_init`, `sem_wait`, and `sem_post`.
- `sem_wait` blocks if the semaphore is 0.
- `sem_post` is called when leaving the critical section and wakes a blocked thread.
- The [[Bounded Buffer Problem]] uses three semaphores: mutex, slot_avail, and item_avail.
- `slot_avail` is initialised to *n*, the buffer length.
- `item_avail` is initialised to 0.
- `mutex` is initialised to 1.
- The producer sleeps when `slot_avail` reaches 0.
- The two forms of [[Inter-process Communication]] are [[Shared Memory]] and [[Message Passing]].
- [[Shared Memory]] is a region mapped into more than one address space.
- With shared memory, a change made by one process is immediately visible to the others.
- [[Amdahl's Law]] caps the speedup from parallelism.
- The cap is set by the fraction of the program that must run serially.
- The serial portion in Amdahl's law is the critical section.
- [[Processor Affinity]] is a thread's preference for the CPU it last ran on.
